headline: Markets Brace for Chip-Sector Test as Iran Tensions and Yield Watch Set Tuesday's Tone
body_html:
Wall Street heads into Tuesday's open carrying the weight of a bruising Monday session, when declining issues outnumbered advancers by a ratio of roughly 342 to 205 across our 549-name universe. Semiconductors bore the sharpest pain, surrendering 2.83% as a group, while energy names slid 1.26% amid a paradox of rising geopolitical risk and an oil market that shrugged off the latest round of U.S. sanctions on Iran-linked traders, pushing crude to a one-week low.

The macro backdrop for Tuesday centers on Treasury markets, where yields held steady overnight as traders positioned ahead of fresh economic data releases. The dollar edged modestly higher as investors weighed the sanctions escalation against Washington's ongoing Treasury buyback program. With Iran vowing retaliation and diplomatic talks between Pakistan and Tehran described as showing meaningful progress, the geopolitical calculus remains fluid — and a direct input into energy and risk-asset pricing at the open.

The session's defining catalyst, however, may come after the close rather than before it: the market is clearly front-running results from the semiconductor space's bellwether, keeping that sector under pressure into Tuesday morning. Consumer names — Monday's lone bright spots alongside homebuilders — will be watched to see whether that defensive rotation has staying power.

briefs.headline: Iran Sanctions Escalation Reshapes Oil-Market Math
briefs.body: The United States moved Monday to sanction an oil trader with alleged Iran links, the latest tightening in a months-long campaign. Despite the move, crude fell to a one-week low as traders judged the near-term supply impact limited. With nearly half of global oil flows now passing through active conflict zones, analysts say the medium-term risk premium is far from priced out.

briefs.headline: Tanzania LNG Project Gains Luster Amid Mideast Conflict
briefs.body: Equinor executives argued Monday that the Iran conflict has made the multibillion-dollar Tanzania LNG development considerably more attractive to buyers and financiers seeking supply diversification away from Gulf routes. The project, long seen as commercially marginal, is drawing renewed scrutiny from energy majors reassessing long-haul supply security in a reconfigured global market.

briefs.headline: Consumer Names Defy Monday's Broad Retreat
briefs.body: While most sectors finished in the red on Monday, consumer-facing stocks staged a notable pocket of resilience. Celsius Holdings led the universe with a 5.01% advance, followed by Vital Farms at 4.82%, American Eagle Outfitters at 4.33%, Dutch Bros at 4.17%, and e.l.f. Beauty at 3.93%. Homebuilders also eked out a 0.60% gain, suggesting selective appetite for domestically oriented names.

briefs.headline: Storage and Database Shares Among Hardest Hit
briefs.body: Monday's technology selloff reached well beyond semiconductors, clipping storage-hardware and database names sharply. Azenta collapsed 12.09% to lead all decliners, while Hims & Hers shed 7.99%, Everpure fell 7.47%, and MongoDB dropped 6.53%. Seagate and Sandisk each lost roughly 6.5%, underscoring broad risk-off sentiment across data-infrastructure plays.

briefs.headline: BlackBerry Positions Robotics as Core Growth Engine
briefs.body: BlackBerry's chief executive said Monday that robotics now ranks among the company's fastest-expanding business lines, a pointed signal of the firm's continuing pivot away from its legacy device identity. The comments arrive as industrial-software players compete aggressively for embedded-systems contracts in autonomous manufacturing and logistics — even as the broader industrials sector finished Monday down 0.81%.

briefs.headline: Dollar and Yields Offer Measured Signals Heading Into the Day
briefs.body: Overnight currency and rates markets delivered a relatively calm handoff to Tuesday's equity open, with the dollar gaining only fractionally and Treasury yields holding steady. Traders indicated they are reserving larger positioning moves for upcoming economic data releases later in the week, keeping fixed-income volatility subdued even as geopolitical headlines continued to generate noise.
